A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ELITE evaluator and benchmark. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including matching material across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations across 18 VLMs, benchmark comparisons, a 963-sample human evaluation, and appendix threshold experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds conventional ASR measurements and a separate 228-sample human study.

M1.justification: The toxicity-weighted ELITE formula, evaluator prompt, four image-text generation approaches, and benchmark construction procedure are unchanged. The additional evaluations do not modify the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same source benchmarks, 4,587-pair ELITE benchmark, 1,054 generated pairs, 11 hazard categories, and four safe/unsafe pairing types. The additional human study samples retained and excluded cases from the existing construction pool without introducing a new domain or safety task.

E2.justification: The reported comparator sets remain unchanged: StrongREJECT, LlamaGuard3-Vision-11B, LlavaGuard-13B, and OpenAI Moderation API for evaluator comparisons, and VLGuard, MM-SafetyBench, and MLLMGuard for benchmark comparisons. Table 4 adds a metric rather than a comparison method.

E3.justification: v3 adds conventional ASR to Table 4 and a separate human evaluation: 110 randomly selected retained samples, 118 excluded samples, at least 20 cases per taxonomy, eight annotators, and three judgments per sample with majority voting. It also evaluates toxicity-score correlations. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Section 4.4 newly names Gemma-3-4B and InternVL2.5-26B, but Table 4 lacks their rows, so those additional model settings cannot be verified.

E4.justification: v3 adds checks of whether benchmark effectiveness persists under conventional ASR, whether toxicity scores align with individual humans, and whether filtering separates human-judged harmful from harmless responses. It also analyzes merely descriptive responses among excluded cases. These substantially extend validation beyond the retained threshold analysis and examples in Appendix A.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly reports Pearson correlations between individual human ratings and ELITE, and between human raters, adding statistical agreement assessment. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the performance comparisons.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results are retained, while Table 4 adds 20 ASR entries, including 68.98% for ELITE on LLaVa-v1.5-7B. New results include evaluator-human correlations of 0.6447–0.7274, human-judged unsafe rates of 67.27% for retained versus 11.86% for excluded samples, and a 52.54% descriptive-response rate among excluded cases. These are substantial new validation results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The StrongREJECT and ELITE scoring equations and E-ASR definition remain mathematically equivalent. Equation 3 only shortens the score notation. No theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same central claims: toxicity-aware evaluation improves human alignment, filtering improves benchmark quality, and generated pairs broaden safety coverage. The rewritten conclusion restates these claims; the added experiments provide support without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges possible bias from selecting the original human dataset around evaluator disagreements. It newly interprets conventional ASR results as evidence against excessive tailoring to ELITE and higher evaluator-human correlations as evidence of more consistent toxicity judgments. These materially extend the interpretation of central validation evidence. Existing limitations concerning evaluator capability and missing multi-turn attacks remain.

D1.justification: Implementation and reproducibility disclosures remain the same, including generation tools, filtering criteria, model cards, evaluator and taxonomy prompts, and appendix annotation guidelines. No new hardware, decoding settings, code release, or data-access instructions are supplied. The additional study's sampling and annotation design is an evaluation-protocol addition.

R1.justification: Related Work adds DecodingTrust by Wang et al. (2023) as an antecedent in LLM safety evaluation. The relationship to StrongREJECT and existing VLM benchmarks remains unchanged. The updated SIUO title and publication details refer to the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: v3 condenses an introductory explanation, rewrites the conclusion and limitations prose, inserts Section 6, and adds acknowledgments and an Impact Statement largely repeating Appendix C. Affiliations and publication information also change. The overall narrative and appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the correlation heatmap in Figure 5 and human-label comparison in Table 8, expands Table 4 with an ASR column, and reorders and marks filtering models in Table 3 and Appendix Table 9. Existing diagrams and appendix examples are retained, with local layout changes and subsequent renumbering.

improvement.justification: The added ASR check and separate human study provide stronger support for benchmark filtering and toxicity scoring, while acknowledging bias in the original human evaluation improves transparency. The gains are limited because comparator superiority is not re-evaluated on the new sample, the added ASR procedure is underspecified, and Section 4.4 names models absent from Table 4. The paper is better supported, but important validation gaps remain.
